**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health.**  

I’d like to invite you to complete the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** today. This brief, 10‑item questionnaire helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week as you adjust to life with your new baby. It’s a standard tool used to screen for postpartum depression and anxiety, and your honest responses will give us valuable insight into your emotional well‑being.

Everything you share is completely confidential, and this is a safe, supportive space for you to speak openly. There are no right or wrong answers—just your personal experience. I’ll ask each question one at a time, and you can answer in whatever words feel most comfortable for you. The whole process takes only a few minutes.

If at any point you feel uneasy or have any questions, please let me know.  

Whenever you’re ready, we can begin with the first question.

**Question 1:**  
In the past seven days, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Honestly, I’ve hardly ever felt like I could laugh or see the funny side of things in the past week.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’m actually finding it hard to laugh or see the humor in things right now. Most days I just feel flat, and even the things that used to make me smile don’t really get to me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
I’ve only felt that way a little bit—maybe a few times in the whole week, but most of the time I just don’t feel much enjoyment or excitement about anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I’ve caught myself blaming myself a lot when something goes wrong—even things that aren’t really my fault. I keep thinking I should be doing more or doing it better, and I feel guilty as a mother for those moments.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I’ve definitely been anxious or worried for no good reason—most days I find myself spiraling with worries that I can’t really shake, even when there’s nothing obvious to be scared about.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I’ve felt scared or panicky for no good reason several times this past week—often enough that it just sits in the back of my mind and makes it hard to relax.
Things have been getting on top of me
Yes, everything feels like it’s piling up. I’m trying to keep up with the baby’s needs, the house, and my own thoughts, but it’s getting overwhelming and I often feel like I’m barely staying afloat.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve definitely been that way. I feel so down that falling asleep has been hard most nights, and even when I do manage to drift off, I wake up once or twice during the night with my thoughts racing. It leaves me feeling even more exhausted the next day.
I have felt sad or miserable
I’ve felt sad and miserable most days this week. It’s hard to shake that low mood, and even the small things that used to lift my spirits just feel heavy right now.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, I’ve found myself crying more often this week—usually once or twice when I feel especially stressed or overwhelmed. It feels like the tears just come out and I can’t stop them, even when I try to pull myself together for the baby.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yes, I’ve had a few fleeting thoughts about hurting myself this past week—just brief moments when I felt overwhelmed and hopeless. I haven’t made any plans or felt any real urge to act on them, but those thoughts have crossed my mind a couple of times.

You have shared that you feel flat, have little enjoyment, blame yourself, feel anxious, overwhelmed, have trouble sleeping, feel sad, cry, and have had fleeting thoughts of self‑harm. It sounds very exhausting and distressing, and I hear how hard it has been for you. <quote>I've had a few fleeting thoughts about hurting myself</quote>
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient reports being unable to laugh or find humor, matching the 'Not at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling enjoyment only a little, most of the week feeling no excitement, matching 'Hardly at all</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame, indicating 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, daily anxiety and worries with no clear cause, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling scared/panicky several times in the past week, often enough to affect relaxation, matching 'Yes, quite a lot'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports difficulty sleeping most nights, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports a few fleeting thoughts about self-harm occurring a couple of times in the past week, matching the 'Sometimes' option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The EPDS total of 27 exceeds the threshold of 14 and the item 10 score of 2 signals a safety concern, prompting an urgent referral. The patient reports persistent <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, excessive <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and passive <sym>suicidal ideation</sym>. These symptoms align with the <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, which require at least five depressive symptoms including depressed mood or anhedonia, present most days for at least two weeks, and occurring during pregnancy or within four weeks postpartum. The combination of mood, cognitive, and functional impairments, plus the safety alert, indicates probable <med>postpartum depression</med> with significant anxiety. This screening suggests the need for immediate clinical evaluation and safety planning. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Contact your <med>primary care provider</med> or a mental health professional today for an urgent evaluation
2. If you feel unsafe or have worsening thoughts of self‑harm, call emergency services (911) or go to the nearest emergency department
3. Develop a safety plan that includes trusted contacts and emergency numbers
4. Practice sleep hygiene: establish a regular bedtime routine, limit caffeine, and ask for help with nighttime infant care
5. Consider joining a <med>postpartum support group</med> or speaking with a therapist experienced in perinatal mental health
6. Discuss with a clinician the possibility of medication (e.g., antidepressants) if appropriate
7. Arrange follow‑up within the next 24‑48 hours to monitor mood and safety
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**

**Client ID:** [Redacted] **Date:** 2025‑10‑07 **Clinician:** [Name, Credentials]

---

### 1. Reported Symptoms & Emotional/Behavioral Concerns
| Item | Client’s Response |
|------|-------------------|
| **Anhedonia / Low mood** | Difficulty laughing, flat affect; minimal enjoyment; persistent sadness/misery; frequent crying. |
| **Self‑blame / Guilt** | Frequent unnecessary self‑blame, feelings of inadequacy as a mother. |
| **Anxiety / Worry** | Daily “worry spirals” without clear trigger; feeling anxious or scared/panic‑like for no good reason. |
| **Overwhelm / Stress** | Perception that responsibilities are “piling up”; feeling barely able to stay afloat. |
| **Sleep disturbance** | Trouble falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings, non‑restorative sleep. |
| **Suicidal ideation** | Fleeting thoughts of self‑harm (no plan, no intent). |

---

### 2. Consistent Patterns Across Answers
- **Persistent low mood** (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9) with loss of pleasure and frequent crying.  
- **Elevated anxiety/panic** (Q4, Q5) and sense of being overwhelmed (Q6).  
- **Self‑critical cognitions** (Q3) indicating guilt and worthlessness.  
- **Sleep disruption** linked to mood and anxiety (Q7).  
- **Brief suicidal thoughts** (Q10) despite lack of intent or plan.

---

### 3. Screening Significance (Post‑partum Depression & Anxiety)
- **Core depressive indicators:** anhedonia, depressed affect, crying, guilt, sleep difficulty.  
- **Anxiety indicators:** excessive worry, panic‑type fear, feeling overwhelmed.  
- **Safety indicator:** passive suicidal ideation (needs immediate safety assessment).  

---

### 4. Highlighted Risk Factors
- **Mood:** Persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, crying spells.  
- **Sleep:** Insomnia/fragmented sleep contributing to exhaustion.  
- **Cognition:** Self‑blame, feelings of inadequacy as a mother.  
- **Anxiety/Panic:** Daily unwarranted worry, panic‑like fear, sense of being “on top of” everything.  
- **Suicidal thoughts:** Fleeting self‑harm thoughts → **Flagged as safety concern**; requires further risk assessment and safety planning.

---

### 5. Screening Observation Summary
The client reports a constellation of depressive symptoms (marked anhedonia, pervasive low mood, frequent crying, guilt, and sleep disturbance) together with significant anxiety (excessive worry, panic‑type fear, feeling overwhelmed). The presence of passive suicidal ideation, though without plan or intent, constitutes a safety concern that warrants immediate further evaluation and a safety plan. Overall, the symptom profile aligns with clinically significant postpartum depression and anxiety warranting comprehensive assessment and appropriate referral for treatment.
